entries.761bb8cd26bb90d953d0dcf1ca4826ae337758f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17830" type="x-p"/> Shall it be told him that I speak? - Shall I dare to whisper even before God? And suppose any one were to accuse me before him for what I have spoken of him, though that has been well intended, how should I be able to stand in his presence? I should be swallowed up in consternation, and consumed with the splendor of his majesty. But in what state art thou? What hast thou been doing? Thou hast arraigned God for his government of the world; thou hast found fault with the dispensations of his providence; thou hast even charged him with cruelty! What will become of Thee?
entries.d4ce1969a31abf51e40f42cf2bbc8d0019da4364: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17831" type="x-p"/> And now men see not the bright light - Mr. Good gives the sense clearer: - "Even now we cannot look at the light <div eID="gen17831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17832" type="x-p"/> When it is resplendent in the heavens. <div eID="gen17832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17833" type="x-p"/> And a wind from the north hath passed along and cleared them." <div eID="gen17833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17834" type="x-p"/> Elihu seems to refer to the insufferable brightness of the sun. Can any man look at the sun shining in his strength, when a clear and strong wind has purged the sky from clouds and vapours? Much less can any gaze on the majesty of God. Every creature must sink before him. What execrably dangerous folly in man to attempt to arraign His conduct!
entries.4f561784640cc7db85fbe79dbcc2d1362e1b6adf: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17835" type="x-p"/> Fair weather cometh out of the north - Is this any version of the original מצפון זהב יאתה mitstsaphon zahab yeetheh? which is rendered by almost every version, ancient and modern, thus, or to this effect: "From the north cometh gold." Calmet justly remarks, that in the time of Moses, Job, and Solomon, and for a long time after, gold was obtained from Colchis, Armenia, Phasis, and the land of Ophir, which were all north of Judea and Idumea; and are in the Scriptures ordinarily termed the north country. "But what relation can there be between, Gold cometh out of the north, and, With God is terrible majesty?" Answer: Each thing has its properties, and proper characteristics, which distinguish it; and each country has its advantages. Gold, for instance, comes from the northern countries; so praises offered to the Supreme God should be accompanied with fear and trembling: and as this metal is from the north, and northern countries are the places whence it must be procured; so terrible majesty belongs to God, and in him alone such majesty is eternally resident. As זהב zahob, which we translate gold, (see <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference>), comes from a root that signifies to be clear, bright, resplendent, etc.; Mr. Good avails himself of the radical idea, and translates it splendor: - "Splendor itself is with God; <div eID="gen17835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17836" type="x-p"/> Insufferable majesty." <div eID="gen17836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17837" type="x-p"/> But he alters the text a little to get this meaning, particularly in the word יאתה yeetheh, which we translate cometh, and which he contends is the pronoun אתה itself; the י yod, as a performative, here being, as he thinks, an interpolation. This makes a very good sense; but none of the ancient versions understood the place thus, and none of the MSS. countenance this very learned critic's emendation.
entries.963af803810699548cbb0be6c3c80c0b75cb235b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17838" type="x-p"/> Touching the Almighty, we cannot find him out - This is a very abrupt exclamation, and highly descriptive of the state of mind in which Elihu was at this time; full of solemnity, wonder, and astonishment, at his own contemplation of this "great First Cause, least understood." The Almighty! we cannot find him out. <div eID="gen17838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17839" type="x-p"/> Excellent in power and in judgment - We must not pretend to comprehend his being, the mode of his existence, the wisdom of his counsels, nor the mysteries of his conduct. <div eID="gen17839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17840" type="x-p"/> He will not afflict - לא יענה la yeanneh, he will not Answer. He will give account of none of his matters to us. We cannot comprehend his motives, nor the ends he has in view.
entries.9b6731c3beb1797eaed63a5bf12dda908507ac7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17841" type="x-p"/> Men do therefore - Therefore men, אנשים anashim, wretched, miserable, ignorant, sinful men, should fear him. <div eID="gen17841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17842" type="x-p"/> He respecteth not any - No man is valuable in his sight on account of his wisdom; for what is his wisdom when compared with that of the Omniscient? Whatever good is in man, God alone is the author of it. Let him, therefore, that glorieth, glory in the Lord. <div eID="gen17842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17843" type="x-p"/> Thus ends the speech of Elihu; a speech of a widely different description, on the whole, from that of the three friends of Job who had spoken so largely before him. In the speeches of Eliphaz, Zophar, and Bildad, there is little besides a tissue of borrowed wise sayings, and ancient proverbs and maxims, relative to the nature of God, and his moral government of the world. In the speech of Elihu every thing appears to be original; he speaks from a deep and comprehensive mind, that had profoundly studied the subjects on which he discoursed. His descriptions of the Divine attributes, and of the wonderful works of God, are correct, splendid, impressive, and inimitable. Elihu, having now come nearly to a close, and knowing that the Almighty would appear and speak for himself, judiciously prepares for and announces his coming by the thunder and lightning of which he has given so terrific and majestic a description in this and the preceding chapter. The evidences of the Divine presence throng on his eyes and mind; the incomprehensible glory and excellency of God confound all his powers of reasoning and description; he cannot arrange his words by reason of darkness; and he concludes with stating, that to poor weak man God must for ever be incomprehensible, and to him a subject of deep religious fear and reverence. Just then the terrible majesty of the Lord appears! Elihu is silent! The rushing mighty wind, for which the description of the thunder and lightning had prepared poor, confounded, astonished Job, proclaims the presence of Jehovah: and out of this whirlwind God answers for and proclaims himself! Reader, canst thou not conceive something of what these men felt? Art thou not astonished, perplexed, confounded, in reading over these descriptions of the thunder of God's power? Prepare, then, to hear the voice of God himself out of this whirlwind.  <chapter eID="Job.37"/> <div eID="gen17843" type="x-p"/>

entries.f22c2c405bcf01b23ddf0d3c22a969e735e27376: <reference osisRef="Job.37.1-Job.5.1">Job 37:1-5   1</reference>  Yea, at this my heart trembleth <div eID="gen8545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8546" type="x-p"/> And tottereth from its place.   2  Hear, O hear the roar of His voice, <div eID="gen8546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8547" type="x-p"/> And the murmur that goeth out of His mouth.   3  He sendeth it forth under the whole heaven, <div eID="gen8547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8548" type="x-p"/> And His lightning unto the ends of the earth.   4  After it roareth the voice of the thunder, <div eID="gen8548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8549" type="x-p"/> He thundereth with the voice of His majesty, <div eID="gen8549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8550" type="x-p"/> And spareth not the lightnings, when His voice is heard.   5  God thundereth with His voice marvellously, <div eID="gen8550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8551" type="x-p"/> Doing great things, incomprehensible to us. <div eID="gen8551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8552" type="x-p"/> Louis Bridel is perhaps right when he inserts after Job 36 the observation: <hi type="italic">L'éclair brille, la tonnerre gronde.</hi> לזאת does not refer to the phenomenon of the storm which is represented in the mind, but to that which is now to be perceived by the senses. The combination שׁמעוּ שׁמוע can signify both hear constantly, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Isa 6:9</reference>, and hear attentively, <reference osisRef="Job.13.17">Job 13:17</reference>; here it is the latter. רגז of thunder corresponds to the verbs Arab. <hi type="italic">rḥz</hi> and <hi type="italic">rjs</hi>, which can be similarly used. The repetition of קול fo noititeper eh five times calls to mind the seven קולות (ἑπτὰ βρονταί) in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1">Psa 29:1</reference>-11. The parallel is הגה, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.2">Job 37:2</reference></hi>, a murmuring, as elsewhere of the roar of the lion and the cooing of the dove. The <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. of ישׁרהוּ refers to the thunder which rolls through the immeasurable breadth under heaven; it is not <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of ישׁר (Schlottm.), for “to give definite direction” (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Ch 32:30</reference>) is not appropriate to thunder, but <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> of שׁרה, to free, to unbind (Ew., Hirz. and most others). What <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.3">Job 37:3</reference></hi> says of thunder, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.3">Job 37:3</reference></hi> says of light, i.e., the lightning: God sends it forth to the edges, πτέρυγες, i.e., ends, of the earth. אחריו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.4">Job 37:4</reference></hi>, naturally refers to the lightning, which is followed by the roar of the thunder; and יעקּבם to the flashes, which, when once its rumble is heard, God does not restrain (עקּב = עכּב of the Targ., and Arab. <hi type="italic">‛aqqaba</hi>, to leave behind, postpone), but causes to flash forth in quick succession. Ewald’s translation: should He not find (prop. <hi type="italic">non investigaverit</hi>) them (the men that are to be punished), gives a thought that has no support in this connection. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.5">Job 37:5</reference></hi> נפלאות, <hi type="italic">mirabilia</hi>, is equivalent to <hi type="italic">mirabiliter</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Dan.8.24">Dan 8:24</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.65.6">Psa 65:6</reference>; Psa 139:14. ולא נדע is intended to say that God’s mighty acts, with respect to the connection between cause and effect and the employment of means, transcend our comprehension.
entries.3591e36a306ae382fd83290a8d2b8f92deee19a5: <reference osisRef="Job.37.6-Job.10.6">Job 37:6-10   6</reference>  For He saith to the snow: Fall towards the earth, <div eID="gen8552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8553" type="x-p"/> And to the rain-shower <div eID="gen8553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8554" type="x-p"/> And the showers of His mighty rain.   7  He putteth a seal on the hand of every man, <div eID="gen8554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8555" type="x-p"/> That all men may come to a knowledge of His creative work.   8  The wild beast creepeth into a hiding-place, <div eID="gen8555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8556" type="x-p"/> And in its resting-place it remaineth.   9  Out of the remote part cometh the whirlwind, <div eID="gen8556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8557" type="x-p"/> And cold from the cloud-sweepers. 10  From the breath of God cometh ice, <div eID="gen8557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8558" type="x-p"/> And the breadth of the waters is straitened. <div eID="gen8558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8559" type="x-p"/> Like אבי, <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference>, and פּשׁ, <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>, הוא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference></hi> (is falsely translated “be earthwards” by lxx, Targ., and Syr.), also belongs to the most striking Arabisms of the Elihu section: it signifies <hi type="italic">delabere</hi> (Jer. <hi type="italic">ut descendat</hi>), a signification which the Arab. <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi> does not gain from the radical signification placed first in Gesenius-Dietrich’s <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>, to breathe, blow, but from the radical signification, to gape, yawn, by means of the development of the meaning which also decides in favour of the primary notion of the Hebr. הוּה, according to which, what was said on <reference osisRef="Job.6.2">Job 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.13">Job 30:13</reference> is to be corrected.<note placement="foot">Arab. <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi> is originally χαίνειν, to gape, yawn, <hi type="italic">hiare</hi>, e.g., <hi type="italic">hawat et - ta‛natu ,</hi> the stab gapes (imperf. <hi type="italic">tahwı̂</hi>, inf. <hi type="italic">huwı̂jun</hi>), “when it opens its mouth” - the Turkish Kamus adds, to complete the picture: like a tulip. Thence next <hi type="italic">hâwijatun</hi>, χαίνουσα χαῖνον, i.e., χᾶσμα = <hi type="italic">hûwatun , uhwı̂jatun , huwâatun , mahwâtun ,</hi> a cleft, yawning deep, chasm, abyss, βάραθρον, <hi type="italic">vorago; hawı̂jatun and hauhâtun</hi> (a reduplicated form), especially a very deep pit or well. But these same words, <hi type="italic">hâwijatun , hûwatun , uhwı̂jatun , mahwâtun ,</hi> also signify, like the usual Arab. <hi type="italic">hawa'â'un</hi>, the χάσμα between heaven and earth, i.e., the wide, empty space, the same as <hi type="italic">'gauwun</hi>. The wider significations, or rather applications and references of <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi>: air set in motion, a current of air, wind, weather, are all secondary, and related to that primary signification as <hi type="italic">samâ</hi>, rain-clouds, rain, grass produced by the rain, to the prim. signification height, heaven, vid., Mehren, <hi type="italic">Rhetorik d. Araber,</hi> S. 107, Z. 14ff. This <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi>, however, also signifies in general: a broad, empty space, and by transferring the notion of “empty” to mind and heart, as the reduplicated forms <hi type="italic">hûhatun</hi> and <hi type="italic">hauhâtun</hi>: devoid of understanding and devoid of courage, e.g., <hi type="italic">Koran</hi> xiv. 44: <hi type="italic">wa - af'i - datuhum hawâun ,</hi> where Bedhâwî first explains <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi> directly by <hi type="italic">chalâ</hi>, emptiness, empty space, i.e., as he adds, <hi type="italic">châlijetun ‛an el - fahm ,</hi> as one says of one without mind and courage <hi type="italic">qalbuhu hawâun .</hi> Thence also <hi type="italic">hauwun</hi>, emptiness, a hole, i.e., in a wall or roof, a dormar-window (<hi type="italic">kauwe , kûwe</hi>), but also with the genit. of a person or thing: their hole, i.e., the space left empty by them, the side not taken up by them, e.g., <hi type="italic">qa‛ada fi hauwihi ,</hi> he set himself beside him. From the signification to be empty then comes (1) <hi type="italic">hawat el - mar'atu ,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">vacua fuit mulier</hi> = <hi type="italic">orba oiberis,</hi> as χήρα, <hi type="italic">vidua</hi>, properly empty, French <hi type="italic">vide;</hi> (2) <hi type="italic">hawâ er - ragulu ,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">vacuus</hi>, <hi type="italic">inanis factus est vir</hi> = <hi type="italic">exanimatus</hi> (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">frg</hi>, he became empty, euphemistic for he died</note>. <div eID="gen8559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8560" type="x-p"/> From this variously applied primary signification is developed the generally known and usual Arab. <hi type="italic">hawâ</hi>, loose and free, without being held or holding to anything one’s self, to pass away, fly, swing, etc., <hi type="italic">libere ferri, labi,</hi> in general in every direction, as the wind, or what is driven hither and thither by the wind, especially however from above downwards, <hi type="italic">labi, delabi, cadere, deorsum ruere.</hi> From this point, like many similar, the word first passes into the signification of sound (as certainly also שׁאה, שא): as anything falling has a full noise, and so on, δουπεῖν, <hi type="italic">rumorem, fragorem edere</hi> (<hi type="italic">fragor</hi> from <hi type="italic">frangi</hi>), hence <hi type="italic">hawat udhnuhu jawı̂jan</hi> of a singing in the ears. <div eID="gen8560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8561" type="x-p"/> Finally, the mental Arab. <hi type="italic">hawan</hi> (perf. <hi type="italic">hawija</hi>, imperf. <hi type="italic">jahwâ</hi> with the acc.), <hi type="italic">animo ad</hi> or <hi type="italic">in aliquid ferri,</hi> is attached to the notion of passing and falling through space (though by no means to <hi type="italic">hiare</hi>, or the supposed meaning “to breathe, blow”). It is used both emotionally of desire, lust, appetites, passions, and strong love, and intellectually of free opinions or assertions springing from mere self-willed preference, caprices of the understanding. - Fl.) <div eID="gen8561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8562" type="x-p"/> The ל of לשּׁלג influences <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference></hi> also. The Hebr. name for rain, גּשׁם (cogn. with Chald. גשׁם, Arab. <hi type="italic">gism</hi>, a body), denotes the rain collectively. The expression <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference></hi> is exceeded in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference></hi>, where מטרות does not signify rain-drops (Ew.), but, like the Arab. <hi type="italic">amtâr</hi>, rain-showers. The wonders of nature during the rough season (חרף, סתיו, Sol 2:11), between the autumnal and vernal equinoxes, are meant; the rains after the autumnal equinox (the early rain), which begin the season, and the rains before the vernal equinox (the late rain, Zec 10:1), which close it, with the falls of snow between, which frequently produce great desolation, especially the proper winter with its frosty winds and heavy showers, when the business of the husbandmen as of the nomads is brought to a stand-still, and every one retreats to his house or seeks a sheltering corner. <div eID="gen8562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> This is the meaning of <reference osisRef="Job.37.7">Job 37:7</reference> : He sealeth up (חתם בּ as <reference osisRef="Job.33.16">Job 33:16</reference>) the hand of all men that they cannot, viz., on account of the cold out of doors, be opened for work, that all people of His work (i.e., thanking Him for their origin as His handiwork, <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job 34:19</reference>) may come to the perception (of Him who doeth all things). The expression is remarkable, and by the insertion of a m may be as easily cleared up as <reference osisRef="Job.33.17">Job 33:17</reference> : לדעת כּל־אנשׁים מעשׂהוּ, in order that each and every one may acknowledge His work; after which even Jer. translates: <hi type="italic">ut noverint singuli opera sua</hi>. The conjecture אנשׁים עשׂהוּ (Schultens junior, Reiske, Hirz.) is inferior to the former (Olsh.) by its awkward <hi type="italic">synecdoche num</hi>. The <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> in <reference osisRef="Job.37.8">Job 37:8</reference> continues the description of what happens in consequence of the cold rainy season; the expression calls to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.104.22">Psa 104:22</reference>, as Job 34:14. does Psa 104:29. The winter is also the time of the stormy and raw winds. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.9">Job 37:9</reference></hi> Elihu means the storms which come across from the great wide desert, <reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>, therefore the south (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Isa 21:1</reference>; Zec 9:14), or rather south-east winds (Hos 13:15), increasing in violence to storms. החדר (properly the surrounded, enclosed space, never the storehouse, - so that <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Psa 135:7</reference> should be compared, - but <hi type="italic">adytum, penetrale,</hi> as Arab. <hi type="italic">chidr ,</hi> e.g., in <hi type="italic">Vita Timuri</hi> ii. 904: after the removal of the superincumbent earth, they drew away <hi type="italic">sitr chidrihâ ,</hi> the curtain of its innermost part, i.e., uncovered its lowest depth) is here the innermost part of the south (south-east), - comp. <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference> חדרי תימן, and <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference> יעטף ימין (so far as יעטף there signifies <hi type="italic">si operiat se</hi>), - especially of the great desert lying to the south (south-east), according to which ארץ חדרך, Zec 9:1, is translated by the Targ. דרומא ארעא. In opposition to the south-east wind, מזרים, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.9">Job 37:9</reference></hi>, seems to mean the north winds; in and of itself, however, the word signifies the scattering or driving, as also in the Koran the winds are called the scatterers, <hi type="italic">dhârijât ,</hi> <hi type="italic">Sur.</hi> li. 1.<note placement="foot">This <hi type="italic">dhârijât</hi> is also differently explained; but the first explanation in Beidhâwi (ii. 183, Fleischer’s edition) is, “the winds which scatter (blow away) the dust and other things.”</note> <div eID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> In מזרים, Reiske, without any ground for it, traces the Arab. <hi type="italic">mirzam</hi> (a name of two stars, from which north wind, rain, and cold are derived); the Targ. also has one of the constellations in view: מכּוּת מזרים (from the window, i.e., the window of the vault of heaven, of the <hi type="italic">mezarim</hi>); Aq., Theod. ἀπὸ μαζούρ (= מזרות, <reference osisRef="Job.38.32">Job 38:32</reference>); lxx ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ἀκρωτηρίων, we know not wherefore. Concerning מנּשׁמת־אל (with causal מן) with reference to the wind, vid., on Job 4:15. יתּן, it gives, i.e., comes to light, is used as in <reference osisRef="Gen.38.28">Gen 38:28</reference>; Pro 13:10. The idea of מוּצק (not <hi type="italic">fusum</hi> from יצק, but <hi type="italic">coarctatum</hi> from צוּק) cannot be doubtful in connection with the antithesis of רחב, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference>, the idea is like <reference osisRef="Job.38.30">Job 38:30</reference> (comp. Mutenebbi: “the flood is bound by bands of ice”); the בּ of בּמוּצק is, as <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">Job 36:32</reference>, the <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae,</hi> used far more extensively in Hebr. than in Arab. as an exponent of the predicate: the breadth of the water is (becomes) straitened (forcibly drawn together).
entries.ab5b40ff3212766b1d7e90166876572fcf671367: <reference osisRef="Job.37.11-Job.13.11">Job 37:11-13 11</reference>  Also He loadeth the clouds with water, <div eID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8565" type="x-p"/> He spreadeth far and wide the cloud of His light, 12  And these turn themselves round about, <div eID="gen8565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8566" type="x-p"/> Directed by Him, that they execute <div eID="gen8566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8567" type="x-p"/> All that He hath commanded them <div eID="gen8567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8568" type="x-p"/> Over the wide earth. 13  Whether for a scourge, or for the good of His earth, <div eID="gen8568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8569" type="x-p"/> Or for mercy, He causeth it to discharge itself. <div eID="gen8569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8570" type="x-p"/> With אף extending the description, Elihu, in the presence of the storm that is in the sky, continually returns to this one marvel of nature. The old versions connect בּרי partly with בּר, <hi type="italic">electus</hi> (lxx, Syr., Theod.) or <hi type="italic">frumentum</hi> (Symm., Jer.), partly with בּרה = בּרר in the signification <hi type="italic">puritas, serenitas</hi> (Targ.); but בּרי is, as Schultens has already perceived, the Hebr.-Arabic רי, Arab. <hi type="italic">rı̂yun , rı̂ j- un</hi> (from רוה = <hi type="italic">riwj</hi>), abundant irrigation, with בּ; and יטריח does not signify, according to the Arab. <hi type="italic">atraha</hi>, “to hurl down,” so that what is spoken of would be the bursting of the clouds (Stick.),<note placement="foot">This “<hi type="italic">a t raha</hi>” is, moreover, a pure invention of our ordinary Arabic lexicons instead of <hi type="italic">ittaraha</hi> (VIII form): (1) to throw one’s self, (2) to throw anything from one’s self, with an <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of the thing. - Fl.</note> but, according to טרח, a burden (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">taraha ala ,</hi> to load), “to burden;” with fluidity (Ew., Hirz., Hahn, Schlottm.), better: fulness of water, He burdens the clouds (comp. <hi type="italic">rawij - un</hi> as a designation of cloud as the place of rain). ענן אורו, His cloud of light, is that that is charged with lightning, and הפיץ has here its Hebr.-Arab. radical signification <hi type="italic">effundere, diffundere,</hi> with a preponderance of the idea not of scattering, but of spreading out wide (Arab. <hi type="italic">faid</hi>, abundance). והוּא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.12">Job 37:12</reference></hi>, refers to the cloud pregnant with lightning; this turns round about (מסבּות, adv. as מסב, round about, 1Ki 6:29) seeking a place, where it shall unburden itself by virtue of His (God’s) direction or disposing (תחבּוּלת, a word belonging to the book of Proverbs; lxx, <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat.</hi> and <hi type="italic">Alex.,</hi> untranslated: εν θεεβουλαθωθ, <hi type="italic">Cod. Sinait.</hi> still more monstrous), in order that they (the clouds full of lightning) may accomplish everything that He commands them over the surface of the earth; ארצה as <reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference>, and the combination תּבל ארצה as <reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Pro 8:31</reference>, comp. ארץ ותבל, Psa 90:2. The reference of the pronominal <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. to men is as inadmissible here as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.4">Job 37:4</reference></hi>. In <reference osisRef="Job.37.13">Job 37:13</reference> two אם have certainly, as <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job 34:29</reference>, two ו, the correlative signification <hi type="italic">sive ... sive</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">in</hi>...<hi type="italic">wa - in</hi>), in a third, as appears, a conditional, but which? According to Ew., Hirz., Hahn, Schlottm., and others, the middle one: if it (the rod) belongs to His land, i.e., if it has deserved it. But even the possessive <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. of לארצו shows that the ל is to be taken as <hi type="italic">dat. commodi:</hi> be it for a rod, be it for the good of His land; which is then followed by a conditional verbal clause: in case He mercifully causes it (the storm) to come, i.e., causes this His land to be overtaken by it (המציא here with the <hi type="italic">acc.,</hi> the thing coming, whereas in <reference osisRef="Job.34.11">Job 34:11</reference> of the thing to be overtaken). The accentuation, indeed, appears to assume a threefold <hi type="italic">sive:</hi> whether He causeth it to discharge itself upon man for punishment, man for mercy, or His earth for good with reference to man. Then Elihu would think of the uninhabited steppe in connection with אם לארצו. Since a conditional אם by the side of two correlatives is hazardous, we decide finally with the lxx, Targ., and all the old versions, in favour of the same rendering of the threefold אם, especially since it corresponds to the circumstances of the case.
entries.240b0d3bf491ca4e3db899a941b4e6bc164a138e: <reference osisRef="Job.37.14-Job.16.14">Job 37:14-16 14</reference>  Hearken unto this, O Job; <div eID="gen8570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> Stand still and consider the wonderful works of God! 15  Dost thou know when God designeth <div eID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8572" type="x-p"/> To cause the light of His clouds to shine? 16  Dost thou understand the balancings of the clouds, <div eID="gen8572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8573" type="x-p"/> The wondrous things of Him who is perfect in knowledge? <div eID="gen8573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8574" type="x-p"/> Job is to stand still, instead of dictating to God, in order to draw from His wondrous acts in nature a conclusion with reference to his mystery of suffering. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.15">Job 37:15</reference></hi> ידע בּ does not, as <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference> (Ew. §217, S. 557), belong together, but בּ is the temporal <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>. שׂוּם is equivalent to שׂים לבּו (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>); עליהם does not refer to נפלאות (Hirz.) or the phenomena of the storm (Ew.), but is intended as neuter (as בּם <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference>, בּהם <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>), and finds in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.15">Job 37:15</reference></hi> its distinctive development: “the light of His clouds” is their effulgent splendour. Without further support, ידע על is to have knowledge concerning anything, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference></hi>; מפלשׂי is also ἁπ. γεγρ.. It is unnecessary to consider it as wrongly written from מפרשׂי, <reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference>, or as from it by change of letter (as אלמנות = ארמנות, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Isa 13:22</reference>). The verb פּלּס signifies to make level, prepare (viz., a way, also weakened: to take a certain way, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.6">Pro 5:6</reference>), once: to weigh, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Psa 58:3</reference>, as <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. from פּלס, a balance (and indeed a steelyard, <hi type="italic">statera</hi>), which is thus mentioned as the means of adjustment. מפלשׂי accordingly signifies either, as synon. of משׁקלי (thus the Midrash, vid., <hi type="italic">Jalkut</hi>, §522), weights (the relations of weight), or even equipoised balancings (Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, and others), Lat. <hi type="italic">quomodo librentur nubes in aëre.</hi><note placement="foot">The word is therefore a metaphor taken from the balance, and it may be observed that the Syro-Arabic, on account of the most extensive application of the balance, is unusually rich in such metaphors. Moreover, the Arabic has no corresponding noun: the <hi type="italic">teflı̂s</hi> (a balance) brought forward by Ges. in his <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi> from Schindler’s <hi type="italic">Pentaglotton</hi>, is a word devoid of all evidence from original sources and from the modern usage of the language, in this signification.</note> מפלאות is also a word that does not occur elsewhere; in like manner דּע belongs exclusively to Elihu. God is called תּמים דּעים (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.36.4">Job 36:4</reference>) as the Omniscient One, whose knowledge is absolute as to its depth as well as its circumference.
entries.67f8e819fd57d81aec32f04fb6d6b5dd4c59ade3: <reference osisRef="Job.37.17-Job.20.17">Job 37:17-20 17</reference>  Thou whose garments became hot, <div eID="gen8574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8575" type="x-p"/> When the land is sultry from the south: 18  Dost thou with Him spread out the sky, <div eID="gen8575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8576" type="x-p"/> The strong, as it were molten, mirror? 19  Let us know what we shall say to Him! - <div eID="gen8576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8577" type="x-p"/> We can arrange nothing by reason of darkness. 20  Shall it be told Him that I speak, <div eID="gen8577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8578" type="x-p"/> Or shall one wish to be destroyed? <div eID="gen8578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8579" type="x-p"/> Most expositors connect <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.17">Job 37:17</reference></hi> with <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference> : (Dost thou know) how it comes to pass that ... ; but      אשׁר after ידע signifies <hi type="italic">quod</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.11.7">Exo 11:7</reference>, not <hi type="italic">quomodo</hi>, as it sometimes occurs in a comparing antecedent clause, instead of כאשׁר, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.13">Exo 14:13</reference>; Jer 33:22. We therefore translate: thou whose ... , - connecting this, however, not with <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference> (vid., e.g., Carey), but as Bolduc. and Ew., with <reference osisRef="Job.37.18">Job 37:18</reference> (where ה before תרקיע is then the less missed): thou who, when the land (the part of the earth where thou art) keeps rest, i.e., in sultriness, when oppressive heat comes (on this <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. vid., Ges. §53, 2) from the south (i.e., by means of the currents of air which come thence, without דּרום signifying directly the south wind), - thou who, when this happens, canst endure so little, that on the contrary the heat from without becomes perceptible to thee through thy clothes: dost thou now and then with Him keep the sky spread out, which for firmness is like a molten mirror? Elsewhere the hemispheric firmament, which spans the earth with its sub-celestial waters, is likened to a clear sapphire <reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Exo 24:10</reference>, a covering <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>, a gauze <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference>; the comparison with a metallic mirror (מוּצק here not from צוּק, <reference osisRef="Job.37.10">Job 37:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference>, but from יצק) is therefore to be understood according to Petavius: <hi type="italic">Coelum aëreum</hi> στερέωμα <hi type="italic">dicitur non a naturae propria conditione, sed ab effectu, quod perinde aquas separet, ac si murus esset solidissimus. </hi> Also in תרקיע lies the notion both of firmness and thinness; the primary notion (root רק) is to beat, make thick, <hi type="italic">stipare</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">rq‛</hi>, to stop up in the sense of <hi type="italic">resarcire</hi>, e.g., to mend stockings), to make thick by pressure. The ל joined with תרקיע is <hi type="italic">nota acc.;</hi> we must not comp. <reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.22">Job 21:22</reference>, as well as <reference osisRef="Job.5.2">Job 5:2</reference>; Job 19:3. <div eID="gen8579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8580" type="x-p"/> Therefore: As God is the only Creator (<reference osisRef="Job.9.8">Job 9:8</reference>), so He is the all-provident Preserver of the world - make us know (הודיענוּ, according to the text of the Babylonians, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> of הודיעני) what we shall say to Him, viz., in order to show that we can cope with Him! We cannot arrange, viz., anything whatever (to be explained according to ערך מלּין, <reference osisRef="Job.32.14">Job 32:14</reference>, comp. “to place,” <reference osisRef="Job.36.19">Job 36:19</reference>), by reason of darkness, viz., the darkness of our understanding, σκότος τῆς διανοίας; מפּני is much the same as <reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference>, but different from <reference osisRef="Job.17.12">Job 17:12</reference>, and חשׁך different from both passages, viz., as it is often used in the New Testament, of intellectual darkness (comp. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.14">Ecc 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.2">Isa 60:2</reference>). The meaning of <reference osisRef="Job.37.20">Job 37:20</reference> cannot now be mistaken, if, with Hirz., Hahn, and Schlottm., we call to mind <reference osisRef="Job.36.10">Job 36:10</reference> in connection with אמר כּי: can I, a short-sighted man, enshrouded in darkness, wish that what I have arrogantly said concerning and against Him may be told to God, or should one earnestly desire (אמר, a modal <hi type="italic">perf.,</hi> as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference></hi>) that (<hi type="italic">an jusserit s. dixerit quis ut</hi>) he may be swallowed up, i.e., destroyed (comp. לבלעו, <reference osisRef="Job.2.3">Job 2:3</reference>)? He would, by challenging a recognition of his unbecoming arguing about God, desire a tribunal that would be destructive to himself.
entries.b814e89ad6fa6052f4f63e65be4b9aefe31af01c: <reference osisRef="Job.37.21-Job.24.21">Job 37:21-24 21</reference>  Although one seeth now the sunlight <div eID="gen8580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8581" type="x-p"/> That is bright in the ethereal heights: <div eID="gen8581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8582" type="x-p"/> A wind passeth by and cleareth them up. 22  Gold is brought from the north, - <div eID="gen8582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8583" type="x-p"/> Above Eloah is terrible majesty. 23  The Almighty, whom we cannot find out, <div eID="gen8583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8584" type="x-p"/> The excellent in strength, <div eID="gen8584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8585" type="x-p"/> And right and justice He perverteth not. 24  Therefore men regard Him with reverence, <div eID="gen8585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8586" type="x-p"/> He hath no regard for all the wise of heart. <div eID="gen8586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8587" type="x-p"/> He who censures God’s actions, and murmurs against God, injures himself - how, on the contrary, would a patiently submissive waiting on Him be rewarded! This is the connection of thought, by which this final strophe is attached to what precedes. If we have drawn the correct conclusion from <reference osisRef="Job.37.1">Job 37:1</reference>, that Elihu’s description of a storm is accompanied by a storm which was coming over the sky, ועתּה, with which the speech, as <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>, draws towards the close, is not to be understood as purely conclusive, but temporal: And at present one does not see the light (אור of the sun, as <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>) which is bright in the ethereal heights (בּהיר again a Hebr.-Arab. word, comp. <hi type="italic">bâhir</hi>, outshining, surpassing, especially of the moon, when it dazzles with its brightness); yet it only requires a breath of wind to pass over it, and to clear it, i.e., brings the ethereal sky with the sunlight to view. Elihu hereby means to say that the God who his hidden only for a time, respecting whom one runs the risk of being in perplexity, can suddenly unveil Himself, to our surprise and confusion, and that therefore it becomes us to bow humbly and quietly to His present mysterious visitation. With respect to the removal of the clouds from the beclouded sun, to which <reference osisRef="Job.37.21">Job 37:21</reference> refers, זהב, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.37.22">Job 37:22</reference></hi>, seems to signify the gold of the sun; <hi type="italic">esh - shemsu bi - tibrin ,</hi> the sun is gold, says Abulola. Oriental and Classic literature furnishes a large number of instances in support of this calling the sunshine gold; and it should not perplex us here, where we have an Arabizing Hebrew poet before us, that not a single passage can be brought forward from the Old Testament literature. But מצּפון is against this figurative rendering of the זהב (lxx νέφη χρυσαυγοῦντα). In <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.4">Eze 1:4</reference> there is good reason for the storm-clouds, which unfold from their midst the glory of the heavenly Judge, who rideth upon the cherubim, coming from the north; but wherefore should Elihu represent the sun’s golden light as breaking through from the north? On the other hand, in the conception of the ancients, the north is the proper region for gold: there griffins (grupe’s) guard the gold-pits of the Arimaspian mountains (Herod. iii. 116); there, from the narrow pass of the Caucasus along the Gordyaean mountains, gold is dug by barbarous races (Pliny, <hi type="italic">h. n. </hi>vi. 11), and among the Scythians it is brought to light by the ants (<hi type="italic">ib</hi>. xxxiii. 4). Egypt could indeed provide itself with gold from Ethiopia, and the Phoenicians brought the gold of Ophir, already mentioned in the book of Job, from India; but the north was regarded as the fabulously most productive chief mine of gold; to speak more definitely: Northern Asia, with the Altai mountains.<note placement="foot">Vid., the art. <hi type="italic">Gold</hi>, S. 91, 101, in Ersch and Gruber. The Indian traditions concerning <hi type="italic">Uttaraguru</hi> (the “High Mountain”), and concerning the northern seat of the god on wealth <hi type="italic">Kuvêra</hi>, have no connection here; on their origin comp. Lassen, <hi type="italic">Indische Alterthumskunde,</hi> i. 848.</note> <div eID="gen8587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8588" type="x-p"/> Thus therefore <reference osisRef="Job.28.1">Job 28:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.28.6">Job 28:6</reference> is to be compared here. <div eID="gen8588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8589" type="x-p"/> What Job describes so grandly and minutely in <reference osisRef="Job.28.1">Job 28:1</reference>, viz., that man lays bare the hidden treasures of the earth’s interior, but that the wisdom of God still transcends him, is here expressed no less grandly and compendiously: From the north cometh gold, which man wrests from the darkness of the gloomy unknown region of the north (צפון, ζόφος, from צפן, cogn. טמן, טמר,<note placement="foot">The verb צּפּה, <hi type="italic">obducere</hi>, does not belong here, but to צפח, and signifies properly to flatten (as רקע, to make thin and thick by striking), comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣfḥ</hi>, to strike on something flat (whence <hi type="italic">el - musâfaha ,</hi> the salutation by striking the hand), and Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣf‛</hi>, to strike with the flat hand on anything, therefore <hi type="italic">diducendo obducere.</hi></note> upon Eloah, on the contrary is terrible majesty (not genitival: terror of majesty, Ew. §293, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), i.e., it covers Him like a garment (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.1">Psa 104:1</reference>), making Him inaccessible (הוד, glory as resounding praise, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference>, like כבוד as imposing dignity). The beclouded sun, <reference osisRef="Job.37.21">Job 37:21</reference> said, has lost none of the intensity of its light, although man has to wait for the removing of the clouds to behold it again. So, when God’s doings are mysterious to us, we have to wait, without murmuring, for His solution of the mystery. While from the north comes gold - <reference osisRef="Job.37.22">Job 37:22</reference> continues - which is obtained by laying bare the interior of the northern mountains, God, on the other hand, is surrounded by inaccessibly terrible glory: the Almighty - thus <reference osisRef="Job.37.23">Job 37:23</reference> completes the thought towards which <reference osisRef="Job.37.22">Job 37:22</reference> tends - we cannot reach, the Great in power, i.e., the nature of the Absolute One remains beyond us, the counsel of the Almighty impenetrable; still we can at all times be certain of this, that what He does is right and good: “Right and the fulness of justice (ורב־ according to the Masora, not ורב-) He perverteth not.” The expression is remarkable: ענּה משׁפּט is, like the Talmudic ענּה דּין, equivalent elsewhere to הטּה משׁפט; and that He does not pervert רב־צדקה, affirms that justice in its whole compass is not perverted by Him; His acts are therefore perfectly and in every way consistent with it: רב־צדקה is the <hi type="italic">abstract</hi>. to צדיק כביר, <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference>, therefore <hi type="italic">summa justitia</hi>. One may feel tempted to draw ומשׁפט to שׂגיא כח, and to read ורב according to <reference osisRef="Prov.14.29">Pro 14:29</reference> instead of ורב, but the expression gained by so doing is still more difficult than the combination לא יענּה...ומשׁפט; not merely difficult, however, but putting a false point in place of a correct one, is the reading לא יענה (lxx, Syr., Jer.), according to which Hirz. translates: He answers, not, i.e., gives no account to man. The accentuation rightly divides <reference osisRef="Job.37.23">Job 37:23</reference> into two halves, the second of which begins with ומשׁפט - a significant <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, on which J. H. Michaelis observes: <hi type="italic">Placide invicem in Deo conspirant infinita ejus potentia et justitia quae in hominibus saepe disjuncta sunt.</hi> <div eID="gen8589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8590" type="x-p"/> Elihu closes with the practical inference: Therefore men, viz., of the right sort, of sound heart, uncorrupted and unaffected, fear Him (יראוּהוּ <hi type="italic">verentur eum,</hi> not יראוּהוּ <hi type="italic">veremini eum</hi>); He does not see (regard) the wise of heart, i.e., those who imagine themselves such and are proud of their לב, their understanding. The <hi type="italic">qui sibi videntur </hi>(Jer.) does not lie in לב (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.21">Isa 5:21</reference>), but in the antithesis. Stick. and others render falsely: Whom the aggregate of the over-wise beholds not, which would be יראנּוּ. God is the subj. as in <reference osisRef="Job.28.24">Job 28:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.21">Job 34:21</reference>, comp. Job 41:26. The assonance of יראוהו and יראה, which also occurs frequently elsewhere (e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.6.21">Job 6:21</reference>), we have sought to reproduce in the translation. <div eID="gen8590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8591" type="x-p"/> In this last speech also Elihu’s chief aim (<reference osisRef="Job.36.2-Job.36.4">Job 36:2-4</reference>) is to defend God against Job’s charge of injustice. He shows how omnipotence, love, and justice are all found in God. When judging of God’s omnipotence, we are to beware of censuring Him who is absolutely exalted above us and our comprehension; when judging of God’s love, we are to beware of interpreting His afflictive dispensations, which are designed for our well-being, as the persecution of an enemy; when judging of His justice, we are to beware of maintaining our own righteousness at the cost of the Divine, and of thus avoiding the penitent humbling of one’s self under His well-meant chastisement. The twofold peculiarity of Elihu’s speeches comes out in this fourth as prominently as in the first: (1) They demand of Job penitential submission, not by accusing him of coarse common sins as the three have done, but because even the best of men suffer for hidden moral defects, which must be perceived by them in order not to perish on account of them. Elihu here does for Job just what in Bunyan (<hi type="italic">Pilgrim’s Progress</hi>) the man in the Interpreter’s house does, when he sweeps the room, so that Christian had been almost choked with the dust that flew about. Then (2) they teach that God makes use of just such sufferings, as Job’s now are, in order to bring man to a knowledge of his hidden defects, and to bless him the more abundantly if he will be saved from them; that thus the sufferings of those who fear God are a wholesome medicine, disciplinary chastenings, and saving warnings; and that therefore true, not merely feigned, piety must be proved in the school of affliction by earnest self-examination, remorseful self-accusation, and humble submission. <div eID="gen8591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8592" type="x-p"/> Elihu therefore in this agrees with the rest of the book, that he frees Job’s affliction from the view which accounts it the evil-doer’s punishment (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.32.3">Job 32:3</reference>). On the other hand, however, he nevertheless takes up a position apart from the rest of the book, by making Job’s sin the cause of his affliction; while in the idea of the rest of the book Job’s affliction has nothing whatever to do with Job’s sin, except in so far as he allows himself to be drawn into sinful language concerning God by the conflict of temptation into which the affliction plunges him. For after Jehovah has brought Job over this his sin, He acknowledges His servant (<reference osisRef="Job.42.7">Job 42:7</reference>) to be in the right, against the three friends: his affliction is really not a merited affliction, it is not a result of retributive justice; it also had not chastisement as its design, it was an enigma, under which Job should have bowed humbly without striking against it - a decree, into the purpose of which the prologue permits us an insight, which however remains unexplained to Job, or is only explained to him so far as the issue teaches him that it should be to him the way to a so much the more glorious testimony on the part of God Himself. <div eID="gen8592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8593" type="x-p"/> With that criticism of Job, which the speeches of Jehovah consummate, the criticism which lies before us in the speeches of Elihu is irreconcilable. The older poet, in contrast with the false doctrine of retribution, entirely separates sin and punishment or chastisement in the affliction of Job, and teaches that there is an affliction of the righteous, which is solely designed to prove and test them. His thema, not Elihu’s (as Simson<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Zur Kritik des B. Hiob</hi>, 1861, S. 34.</note> with Hengstenberg thinks), is <hi type="italic">the mystery of the Cross.</hi> For the Cross according to its proper notion is suffering ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης (or what in New Testament language is the same, ἕνεκεν Χριστοῦ). Elihu, however, leaves sin and suffering together as inseparable, and opposes the false doctrine of retribution by the distinction between disciplinary chastisement and judicial retribution. The Elihu section, as I have shown elsewhere,<note placement="foot">Vid., Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real-Encyklopädie,</hi> art. <hi type="italic">Hiob</hi>, S. 119.</note> has sprung from the endeavour to moderate the bewildering boldness with which the older poet puts forth his idea. The writer has felt in connection with the book of Job what every Christian must feel. Such a maintaining of his own righteousness in the face of friendly exhortations to penitence, as we perceive it in Job’s speeches, is certainly not possible where “the dust of the room has flown about.” The friends have only failed in this, that they made Job more and more an evil-doer deservedly undergoing punishment. Elihu points him to vainglorying, to carnal security, and in the main to those defects from which the most godly cannot and dare not claim exemption. It is not contrary to the spirit of the drama that Job holds his peace at these exhortations to penitence. The similarly expressed admonition to penitence with which Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.4.1">Job 4:1</reference>, begins, has not effected it. In the meanwhile, however, Job is become more softened and composed, and in remembrance of his unbecoming language concerning God, he must feel that he has forfeited the right of defending himself. Nevertheless this silent Job is not altogether the same as the Job who, in Job 40 and 42, forces himself to keep silence, whose former testimony concerning himself, and whose former refusal of a theodicy which links sin and calamity together, Jehovah finally sets His seal to. <div eID="gen8593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8594" type="x-p"/> On the other hand, however, it must be acknowledged, that what the introduction to Elihu’s speeches, <reference osisRef="Job.32.1-Job.32.5">Job 32:1-5</reference>, sets before us, is consistent with the idea of the whole, and that such a section as the introduction leads one to expect, may be easily understood really as a member of the whole, which carries forward the dramatic development of this idea; for this very reason one feels urged to constantly new endeavours, if possible, to understand these speeches as a part of the original form. But they are without result, and, moreover, many other considerations stand in our way to the desired goal; especially, that Elihu is not mentioned in the epilogue, and that his speeches are far behind the artistic perfection of the rest of the book. It is true the writer of these speeches has, in common with the rest of the book, a like Hebraeo-Arabic, and indeed Hauranitish style, and like mutual relations to earlier and later writings; but this is explained from the consideration that he has completely blended the older book with himself (as the points of contact of the fourth speech with <reference osisRef="Job.28.1">Job 28:1</reference> and the speeches of Jehovah, show), and that to all appearance he is a fellow-countryman of the older poet. There are neither linguistic nor any other valid reasons in favour of assigning it to a much later period. He is the second issuer of the book, possibly the first, who brought to light the hitherto hidden treasure, enriched by his own insertion, which is inestimable in its relation to the history of the perception of the plan of redemption. <div eID="gen8594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8595" type="x-p"/> We now call to mind that in the last (according to our view) strophe of Job’s last speech. <reference osisRef="Job.31.35-Job.31.37">Job 31:35-37</reference>, Job desires, yea challenges, the divine decision between himself and his opponents. His opponents have explained his affliction as the punishment of the just God; he, however, is himself so certain of his innocence, and of his victory over divine and human accusation, that he will bind the indictment of his opponents as a crown upon his brow, and to God, whose hand of punishment supposedly rests upon him, will he render an account of all his steps, and go forth as a prince to meet Him. That he considers himself a צדיק is in itself not censurable, for he is such: but that he is מצדק נפשׁו מאלהים, i.e., considers himself to be righteous in opposition to God, who is no angry with him and punishes him; that he maintains his own righteousness to the prejudice of the Divine; and that by maintaining his own right, places the Divine in the shade, - all this is explainable as the result of the false idea which he entertains of his affliction, and in which he is strengthened by the friends; but there is need of censure and penitence. For since by His nature God can never do wrong, all human wrangling before God is a sinful advance against the mystery of divine guidance, under which he should rather humbly bow. But we have seen that Job’s false idea of God as his enemy, whose conduct he cannot acknowledge as just, does not fill his whole soul. The night of temptation in which he is enshrouded, is broken in upon by gleams of faith, in connection with which God appears to him as his Vindicator and Redeemer. Flesh and spirit, nature and grace, delusion and faith, are at war within him. These two elements are constantly more definitely separated in the course of the controversy; but it is not yet come to the victory of faith over delusion, the two lines of conception go unreconciled side by side in Job’s soul. The last monologues issue on the one side in the humble confession that God’s wisdom is unsearchable, and the fear of God is the share of wisdom appointed to man; on the other side, in the defiant demand that God may answer for his defence of himself, and the vaunting offer to give Him an account of all his steps, and also then to enter His presence with the high feeling of a prince. If now the issue of the drama is to be this, that God really reveals Himself as Job’s Vindicator and Redeemer, Job’s defiance and boldness must be previously punished in order that lowliness and submission may attain the victory over them. God cannot acknowledge job as His servant before he penitently acknowledges as such the sinful weakness under which he has proved himself to be God’s servant, and so exhibits himself anew in his true character which cherishes no known sin. This takes place when Jehovah appears, and in language not of wrath but of loving condescension, and yet earnest reproof, He makes the Titan quite puny in his own eyes, in order then to exalt him who is outwardly and inwardly humbled.  <chapter eID="Job.37"/> <div eID="gen8595" type="x-p"/>

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection <ns0:note place="bottom">Heb <ns0:hi>for a rod,</ns0:hi> to scourge or correct men by immoderate showers. Or, <ns0:hi>for a Tribe,</ns0:hi> or certain Portion of Land, which God intends particularly to punish in that kind.</ns0:note>, or for his land <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> For God's Land where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by he understands, either 1. the Land which he favoureth, and where his Servants live, such as <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> was, which for that rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son God blessed with rain, as is noted, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 11. 12. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68. 9, 10. But in <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s time God's People were not in <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> but in <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> where little or no Rain fell. or 2. the uninhabited or desert parts of the World, which may be called <ns0:hi>Gods Land</ns0:hi> peculiarly, because it is immediately and onely under Gods care as being not regarded nor possessed by any man. For it is noted as a special act of God's Providence that he causeth Rain to fall upon such places, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 38. 26, 27<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Or 3. <ns0:hi>his Earth,</ns0:hi> as it may be rendred, to wit, the whole Earth, which is said to be <ns0:hi>the Lords,</ns0:hi> Psal. 24. 1. & 50. 12. and which may be here opposed to <ns0:hi>a Tribe,</ns0:hi> or little part of the Earth. And so this may note a general judgment by excessive Rains inflicted up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the whole Earth and all its Inhabitants, even the universal De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />luge, which then was in a manner of fresh memory, which came in a great measure out of the Clouds. And thus these two first members speak of correction, and the last of Mercy.</ns0:note>, or for mercy <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">For the comfort and benefit of Mankind by cooling and cleansing the Air and refreshing and improving all the fruits of the Earth, and other ways.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. Hearken unto this, O Job: stand still, and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sider the wondrous works of God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">If there be so much matter of wonder and adoration in the most obvious and sensible works of God, how wonderful must his deep and secret counsels and judgments be? And therefore it would better become thee humbly to admire, and quietly to submit to them, than to murmur or quarrel with them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Dost thou know when God disposed them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To wit, the things before mentioned, the Clouds, Rain, Snow, Thunder and Lightning, and other Meteors. Did God ask coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel from thee to acquaint thee with his counsels in the producing and ordering of them, when and where, and in what manner he should dispose them? God ordereth all these things not as it pleaseth thee, but as he thinks meet; and in like manner he disposeth of all humane affairs, and of thine among the rest.</ns0:note>, and caused the light of his cloud to shine <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which may be understood either 1. of the light of the Sun breaking through the Clouds, when it is most glorious and comfortable. But though this light break through the Clouds, yet it is very improper to call it <ns0:hi>the light of the Clouds.</ns0:hi> Or, 2. The Lightning, which is properly so called, a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> being produced by and in a Cloud. Or, 3. The Rain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bow, which is a lightsom and glorious work of God, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore not likely to be omitted in this place<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and which is seated in a Cloud which also may well be called God's Cloud, because therein God puts <ns0:hi>his Bow,</ns0:hi> as the Rainbow is called. <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 9. 13.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. Dost thou know the balancings <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">How God doth as it were weigh and suspend the Clouds in Balances, so that although they are ponderous and full of Water, yet they are by his power kept up in the thin Air from falling down upon us in spouts and floods, as sometimes they have done and generally would do, if not over-ruled by an higher Providence.</ns0:note> of the clouds, the wondrous works of him which is perfect <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Who exactly knows the weight. These are effects and evidences of his infinite power and knowledge.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. How thy garments <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> warm <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">How and why thy garments keep thee warm; of which as there are some natural causes, so it is certain that they are not sufficient to do it without Gods blessing, as experience shews, <ns0:hi>Hagg.</ns0:hi> 1. 6.</ns0:note>, when he quiet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth the earth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Air about the earth.</ns0:note> By the South <ns0:hi>w<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nd</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which though sometimes it brings Tempests, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. yet commonly it ushereth in hot wea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 12. 55. as the North-wind brings cold, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. Or, <ns0:hi>from the South wind,</ns0:hi> i. e. from the Tempest which was noted to come out of the South, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. Heb. <ns0:hi>from</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>by the South,</ns0:hi> i. e. by the Suns coming into the Southern parts, which makes the Air quiet and warm.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. Hast thou with him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 1. 6.</ns0:note> spread out the skie <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Wast thou his co worker or assistant in spreading out the Skie like a Tent or Canopy over the Earth? Or, canst thou spread out such another Skie? Then indeed thou mayst with some colour pretend to be privy to his co<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nsels and to judge of his works.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> strong <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which though it be very thin and transparent, yet is also firm and compact and stedfast, and of great force when it is p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> up.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> as a molten looking glass <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Made of Brass or Steel, as the manner then was.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. Teach us what we shall say unto him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Unto God, either by way of Apology for thee: or rather by way of debate and disputation with him about his counsels and ways; about which we know not what to say, and therefore are willing to be taught by thee who pretendest to such exquisit know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge of these matters. So it is a reproof of his presumption and arrogance.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> we cannot <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 32. 14.</ns0:note> order <ns0:hi>our speech</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">we know neither with what words or matter, nor in what method and manner, to maintain discourse with him, or plead against him. The words <ns0:hi>our speech,</ns0:hi> are easily understood out of the former Clause of the Verse.</ns0:note> by reason of darkness <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Both because of the dark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the matter, God's counsels and ways being a great depth<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and far out of our reach; and because of the darkness or blindness of our minds.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. Shall it be told him that I speak <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>that I will speak.</ns0:hi> Shall I send, or who d<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>re carry a Challenge from me to God, or a Message that I am ready and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sirous to debate with him concerning his proceedings? This in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deed thou hast done in effect, but far be such presumption from me</ns0:note>? if a man speak <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">If a Man should be so bold and venturous to enter the Lists with God.</ns0:note>, surely he shall be swallowed up <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">With the sense of God's infinite Majesty and spotless Purity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. And <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>For,</ns0:hi> as this Particle is oft rendred; the following words containing a reason of those which go before.</ns0:note> now <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This Particle is either 1. a note of time, and so it intimates a sudden change which then was in the Weather, which having been very dark beg<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>n now to clear up: Or rather 2. a note of in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>erence to usher in the argument.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> see not <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either 1. do not observe (as <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> is oft used) nor consider these glorious works of God. or 2. cannot behold, or at least not gaze upon it.</ns0:note> the bright light which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the clouds <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in the Skies:</ns0:hi> For the Hebrew word signifies both <ns0:hi>Clouds</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Skies.</ns0:hi> This is to be understood, either 1. of bright and lightsome Clouds: or rather 2. of the Sun, which is oft and emphatically called <ns0:hi>light,</ns0:hi> as was noted before, and here <ns0:hi>the bright light:</ns0:hi> which men <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ftimes cannot behold, either when it is covered with a black and thick Cloud; or when as it follows, the Skie is very clear, and consequently the Sun shine is very bright And therefore it is not strange if we cannot see God, who dwellet in darkness, 1 Kings 8. 12. nor discern his counsels and ways; which are covered with great obscurity, and if we dare not ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proach to him with whom is, as it here follows, terrible Majesty, and if we presume to do so, we must needs be swallowed up, as was said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20.</ns0:note>, but the wind passeth <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>when</ns0:hi> (as this Particle is oft used) <ns0:hi>the wind passeth.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> and cleanseth them <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either the Clouds, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> cleanseth the Air from them: or the Skies by driving away those Clouds which darkned it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">H<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>b. <ns0:hi>gold.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Fair weather <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, when (which Particle may well be understood out of the foregoing Verse; and so this may be a further description of the time when men cannot see or gaze upon the Sun, namely when) <ns0:hi>fair Weather,</ns0:hi> &c. Heb. <ns0:hi>Gold,</ns0:hi> either 1. properly. And so this may be noted as another wonderful work of God that the choicest of Metals, to wit, Gold should be found in and fetched out of the bowels of cold northern Countreys. Or 2. Metaphorically, as this word is oft used of bright and shining things; as we read of <ns0:hi>golden Oyl,</ns0:hi> Zech. 4. 12. and we call happy times <ns0:hi>golden Days.</ns0:hi> And so bright and fair Weather may well be called <ns0:hi>golden,</ns0:hi> because then the Sun gilds the Air and Earth with its beams, which also are called by Poets <ns0:hi>golden B<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>ms.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> cometh out of the north <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From the Northern Winds which scatter the Clouds, and clear the Skie, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 25. 23.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> with God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> terrible Majesty <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And therefore we neither can nor may approach too near to him, nor speak presumptuously or irreverently to him or of him. And so this is the Application of what he had now said<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> that we could not see the Sun, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> much less God: and withal it is an Epiphonema or Conclusion of the whole foregoing Discourse. Those glorious works of his which I have described, are Testimonies of that great and terrible Majesty which is in him; which should cause us to fear and reverence him, and not to behave our selves so insolently to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards him, as <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> hath done.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. <ns0:hi>Touching</ns0:hi> the Almighty, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Tim. 6. 16.</ns0:note> we cannot find him out <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To wit, to perfection, as it is expressed, <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 11. 7. We can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not comprehend him: his Being, Power, Wisdom, Justice, and his counsels proceeding from them are past our finding out: and therefore it is most absurd and intolerable that thou, O <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> presumest to censure what th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>u dost not understand.</ns0:note>, he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 36. 5.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> excellent in power <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore as he doth not need any unrighteous action to advance himself, so he cannot do it, because all such things are acts and evidences of impotency or weakness.</ns0:note>, and in judgment <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the just and righteous administra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of judgment, as this word is oft used, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s the thing it self, and the following words plainly evince. And this he adds to intimate that although God had indeed a Power to crush <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> or any other Man, yet he never did nor can exercise that power unjustly or ty<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rannically, as <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> seemed to insinuate.</ns0:note>, and in plenty of justice <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In great and perfect Justice, such as no Man can justly reproach.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Lam. 3. 33.</ns0:note> he will not afflict <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">To wit, without just cause, and above measure: as it may and must be limited both from the foregoing words, and from <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s complaint which was of that very thing; and from the nature of the thing, because otherwise this Proposition that <ns0:hi>God will not afflict,</ns0:hi> is not simply and universally true. Or these last words may be joyned with the former; and so some render the place, <ns0:hi>He is excellent in Power, and</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>but,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>yet, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>e will not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> any Man <ns0:hi>with judgment and much</ns0:hi> (i. e. too much) <ns0:hi>justice,</ns0:hi> i. e. with extremity or rigo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>r of Justice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:419" />24. Men do therefore fear him <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>For this cause,</ns0:hi> to wit, because of God's infinite and excellent Perfections, and especially those mentioned in the foregoing Verse, <ns0:hi>men do,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>should</ns0:hi> (for the future Tense is oft used potentially as He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bricians know) <ns0:hi>fear</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>reveren<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> him,</ns0:hi> and humbly submit to him, and not presume to quarrel or dispute with him, as thou O <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> hast done.</ns0:note>: he respecteth not <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>He doth not,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>will not behold,</ns0:hi> to wit, with respect or approbation, he beholdeth them afar off with scorn and contempt.</ns0:note> any <ns0:hi>that are</ns0:hi> wise of heart <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Such as are wise in their own eyes, that lean to their own understandings, and despise all other men in comparison of them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves, and scorn all their counsels, that are so puffed up with the opinion of their own wisdom, that they dare contend with their Maker, and presume to censure his counsels and actions. Which he hereby intimates to be <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s fault, and to be the true reason why God did not respect nor regard him, nor his Prayers and Tears, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> complained. And so this is also a Tacit advice and exhorta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion to <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> to be humble and little in his own eyes, if ever he ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pected or desired any favour from God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
